candidates.statement: Clinical trials to support a finding of efficacy for a non-opioid analgesic should be randomized, 105 double-blind, superiority trials. The trials should include repeat-dose design as appropriate. 106 Treatment duration should be based on the pain model used to support the proposed indication 107 sought but should be no fewer than 24 hours for products that are not limited to a single dose. 108 The primary endpoint should be based on the change in pain intensity over a suitable time period 109 based on the pain model used in the trial and the product’s expected duration of pain relief; 110 however, the time period assessed does not have to be for the full duration of the pain. After 111 evaluation of the primary endpoint, we recommend continued evaluation of both safety and 112 efficacy, for evidence of sustained effect, which may be relevant to acute pain lasting up to 30 113 days. 114
candidates.context: For acute pain, it is common to use an analysis such as the Sum of Pain Intensity Difference 116 (SPID) over a prespecified time period that reflects the expected duration of treatment effect of 117 the product. Demonstrating superiority to a comparator is important in non-opioid analgesic 118 trials because the primary endpoint, pain intensity, can be influenced by study design factors 119 such as the use of rescue medication and placebo effect. As a result, a noninferiority trial 120 showing no difference between analgesic treatments could mean that neither product worked in 121

candidates.statement: Protocols should prespecify allowed rescue medications. Depending on the pain condition being 128 studied, rescue medications might include nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs or, in clinical 129 settings in which opioids are typically required for adequate pain relief, opioids may be 130 considered. Protocols should also prespecify the frequency, amount, and threshold of pain at 131 which allowable rescue medication(s) can be administered. This is particularly important in 132 placebo-controlled trials where increased use of rescue medication in the control group may 133 diminish the study drug’s treatment effect, leading to a conclusion of ineffectiveness. The 134 statistical analysis plan should describe how discontinuations caused by inadequate pain control 135 will be handled. The concept of rescue use, including the prospective plan in the effectiveness 136 analysis to assess its use, as well as how the data support the overall indication, is important and 137 is discussed further in section III. A. 3. below, under Secondary Efficacy Endpoints. 138

In 123 some cases, the test treatment and control (placebo or a different analgesic drug) may also be 124 added to background therapy (an “add-on study”). The background therapy could be specified or 125 caregiver selected. 126 3. Outcome Measures to Obtain an Acute Pain Analgesic Indication 140

candidates.statement: In general, an assessment of pain intensity is the primary outcome measure to establish the 144 efficacy of an analgesic intended to manage acute pain. Efficacy endpoints (e.g., change in pain 145 intensity) in a non-opioid analgesic trial should reflect a direct rating of pain intensity by the 146 subject for all settings in which the subject can communicate in a reliable manner. We 147 recommend using a well-defined and reliable patient-reported outcome measure of the subject’s 148 pain intensity. 6 The selected instrument should have the subject assess their pain at the time of 149 the assessment (i.e., without using a recall period). Generally, a numerical rating scale is the 150 appropriate measure. 151
candidates.context: Primary Efficacy Endpoint 142 We recommend that sponsors take frequent pain intensity measurements at preselected time 153 points during the trial to accurately measure the effect of a non-opioid analgesic and that effect 154 over time (e.g., every hour for X number of hours, then every 4 hours for X number of hours). 155 All pain intensity measurements, including at baseline, should be obtained before rescue drug 156 administration. In general, the frequency of pain intensity assessment is greater with initial drug 157 administration, early post-event (e.g., post-injury or surgery), when pain may be more intense. 158 The primary efficacy analysis should compare the SPID between treatments at a prespecified 159 time point that, at a minimum, includes the duration of drug effect, and may extend beyond this 160

candidates.statement: We discourage using a primary endpoint that is based on pain relief (i.e., decrease in pain) rather 166 than pain intensity (i.e., how bad the pain is), as pain relief scales require subjects to report 167 current pain relative to their prior pain experience and may be influenced by other factors such as 168 concurrent adverse reactions, and may be limited by patients’ ability to recall their prior 169 experience of pain. Additionally, sponsors should generally avoid using composite scales that 170 are composed of multiple domains (e.g., pain, function, sleep) as the primary outcome measure 171 in a non-opioid analgesic trial. Such multiple domain scales may be difficult to interpret across a 172 population, as the same change in overall score can be based on differing patterns of response to 173 the individual domain scores. For example, an overall score may be higher at baseline, reflecting 174 poor sleep (with functional consequences), with improvement in the score reflecting 175 improvement in sleep, such as might be seen with a sedating drug that does not provide 176 substantive pain control. Multi-item scales, where the items all relate to pain (e.g., pain at rest or 177 with movement), may be useful depending on the type of pain being studied. 178
candidates.context: duration. For example, a non-opioid analgesic with an expected 4- to 6-hour duration of action 161 might have the primary efficacy analysis performed at 24 hours post-dose (SPID24), but 162 secondary efficacy analyses may also be performed at 6 and 12 hours post dose (SPID6 and 163 SPID12, respectively) to evaluate pain control during the recommended dosing interval. 164 Secondary Efficacy Endpoints 180

candidates.statement: Secondary outcome measures are important to fully characterize the efficacy of a non-opioid 182 analgesic and should support the primary efficacy endpoint. These secondary outcome measures 183 include measurement of time to onset of pain relief and time to rescue or request for next dose of 184 the study drug. Other informative secondary outcome measures include assessment of use of 185 rescue medications, physical function, and patient global impression of change of pain. 186
candidates.context: Secondary Efficacy Endpoints 180 To measure time to onset of pain relief, FDA has accepted the “two stopwatch method.” In this 188 method, patients are instructed to stop the first stopwatch when they first perceive any analgesic 189 effect and instructed to stop the second stopwatch when they perceive a meaningful amount of 190 analgesia, which may be translated into a description in labeling of median time to meaningful 191 pain relief. FDA remains open to discussion and consideration of approaches beyond the “two 192 stopwatch method” to assess the time to onset of pain relief, which is particularly important to 193 establish if there is an expectation of rapid onset of action (e.g., intravenous formulation). 194

candidates.statement: Use of rescue medication can inform important properties of the drug and should be carefully 206 considered in the design of the study so as not to jeopardize the validity of the study. A sooner- 207 than-expected first use of rescue medication may suggest that the investigational drug has a 208 delayed onset of pain relief. Time to second use of rescue medication may be informative when 209 considering dosing interval for the investigational drug and supplement knowledge of the drug’s 210 pharmacokinetic properties. If the time to second use of rescue medication is earlier than 211 expected based upon drug exposure, waning efficacy can be considered a potential issue. 212
candidates.context: • The pain intensity measurements before the rescue medication was used and throughout 203 the dosing interval (e.g., evaluating SPID over the course of expected duration of action) 204 Endpoints Associated with Reducing or Eliminating Opioid Use 214

candidates.statement: As discussed further below, total elimination of opioid or a numerical reduction in the number of 216 doses, dose per day, or duration of opioid use may support the efficacy of the investigational 217 drug in alleviating pain. In order to support a clinical benefit of a reduction in opioid use that 218 would be described in labeling, sponsors should demonstrate a direct patient benefit, such as 219 clinically meaningful reduction in the incidence and/or severity of opioid-induced adverse 220 reactions. See section III. B. below. 221

candidates.statement: When monitoring safety during clinical trials, sponsors should consider the nature of the drug 232 and the trial population. Sponsors may also need to include subject discontinuation and/or study 233 stopping criteria in protocols, depending on the expected safety profile of a non-opioid analgesic. 234
candidates.context: 4. Safety Considerations–Clinical Trial Elements 230 Appropriate assessment of both effectiveness and safety relies on accurate and complete capture 236 of the reason for subject discontinuation. Sponsors should assure that when a subject 237 discontinues study drug or withdraws from the trial that the specific reason is obtained. 238 Investigators should be prompted to provide detailed information, with specific causes rather 239 than report terms such as “other,” “subject request,” “investigator decision,” or other such 240 nonspecific categories. Sponsors also should ensure that case report forms are designed to 241 accurately capture the reason for patient discontinuation. 242

candidates.statement: The size of the safety database needed to support approval for an acute pain indication depends 244 on a number of factors, including whether the drug is a new molecular entity or a reformulation 245 of an approved drug substance. In addition, a nonclinical safety finding or safety data from early 246 clinical studies suggesting a potential serious adverse reaction may necessitate enlargement of 247 the safety database to better define the safety profile of the proposed product. Safety 248 assessments should continue as appropriate after dosing is completed, with consideration of 249 patient population and setting (i.e., inpatient versus outpatient). 250

candidates.statement: Apart from discharge by a health care facility without opioids, reduction in dosage and/or 320 duration of opioid use alone is not likely to be adequate to support description in labeling. To 321 include a reduction in opioid use in labeling, the reduction claim should be associated with a 322 direct patient benefit such as (1) reduced time to recovery of function, such as more rapid 323 mobility and/or earlier ability to participate in rehabilitation or other clinically meaningful 324 functional outcomes, or (2) a relevant decrease in opioid-related adverse reactions such as less 325 sedation, fewer gastrointestinal side effects (such as constipation), or other adverse reactions. If 326 these types of clinical benefits are adequately demonstrated in clinical trials, language in the 327 labeling delineating these benefits could be included. 328
candidates.context: c. Product reduces patient exposure to opioid analgesics with direct clinical 317 benefit to the patient 318 3. Data to Support Language in Labeling Describing Clinically Meaningful 330 Reductions in Opioid Analgesic Use 331

candidates.statement: To support language describing clinically meaningful reductions in opioid analgesic use in 333 product labeling for any of the categories described above, sponsors should provide data from at 334 least two adequate and well-controlled trials. As described in section III. B. 2. above, examples 335 of clinically meaningful outcomes include not requiring opioids for a pain model where opioid 336 use is usually required, or, where use of opioids is still needed, showing reduced opioid dose 337 requirements in concert with either a shortening of time to mobility (e.g., following orthopedic 338 surgery) or a reduction in the frequency of major complications of opioid treatment, such as 339 delirium in an elderly population or a reduction in opioid-related adverse reactions. 340
candidates.context: 3. Data to Support Language in Labeling Describing Clinically Meaningful 330 Reductions in Opioid Analgesic Use 331 FDA also encourages sponsors to include open-label extensions with follow-up assessment of 342 opioid analgesic utilization (e.g., 30 days after discharge following a surgical procedure) to 343 assess whether patients have been taking opioid analgesics during the period of extension. 344
